assessment.nobel_worthiness: Changed how economists and policymakers understand technology, trade and labour demand. It combines the task-based view of work, the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium, and well-identified evidence on local labour market adjustment to import competition. Strong policy relevance and a large empirical and theoretical follow-on literature.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Hanson and Katz are the core credits: Autor for tasks and the China shock, Hanson for the trade-shock design, Katz for the long-run skill-premium framework. The task framework also rests on co-authors outside the credited list, and Dorn is a major co-author of the trade-shock work, so a three-person cap leaves some credit unassigned. The 2023 and 2024 prizes covered adjacent labour and technology topics, which may affect timing but not merit.
assessment.maturity: The skill-premium work is about three decades old and the task model over twenty years old. The China shock papers are over a decade old and have been replicated and extended across countries.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from recently honoured work on technology, inequality and gender in labour markets.
Debate over the persistence and magnitude of trade-shock effects and over how much of polarization is due to tasks versus other forces.
Credit division among Autor, Hanson, Katz and Dorn.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Estimation of demand in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, together with dynamic industry models, became the standard empirical toolkit for merger analysis, antitrust and competition policy. The methodological contribution is deep and the practical impact is large.
assessment.attribution: BLP (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes 1995) is a clear core. Pakes also has foundational dynamic work (the Ericson–Pakes framework and the dynamic estimation papers). Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are credited in the candidate but sit at the edges of a three-person cap.
assessment.maturity: About three decades of use across industrial organization, trade and public economics. The impact is well established.
uncertainties: Choice between a demand-estimation award (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) and one that includes Bresnahan's earlier contributions.
Weight to give structural methods versus the design-based approaches recently honoured.
Some of the dynamic-model estimation literature is still maturing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Created the empirical law-and-finance field by linking legal institutions, investor protection and financial development across countries. It reshaped corporate finance, comparative institutions and development, and gave economists measurable institutional variables. Its influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: The legal-origins and investor-protection papers (La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer, Vishny) form a single clear body of work. Shleifer's broader contributions span many fields. Vishny's most distinctive contributions lie elsewhere, so a three-person selection is reasonable but leaves out a co-author.
assessment.maturity: Core papers date from 1997–2008 and have had a long period of replication and critique.
uncertainties: The legal-origins hypothesis has been strongly challenged on identification and on the stability of the results.
Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson).
Whether the committee sees the cross-country identification as credible enough, and how it weighs non-scientific considerations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel estimators (Arellano–Bond, Arellano–Bover, Blundell–Bond) are among the most widely used tools in applied economics, with large and durable effects on empirical practice in growth, finance, labour and industrial organization. Methodological prizes are well established (Engle/Granger, Heckman/McFadden, Angrist/Imbens).
assessment.attribution: The three credited names map directly to the key estimators. Arellano is central to panel-data theory more broadly. Blundell has much additional work on labour supply and consumption, which strengthens the case but complicates the citation.
assessment.maturity: The core papers are from 1991–1998 and are very mature. Practical weaknesses, such as instrument proliferation, are well known.
uncertainties: Whether the committee values a methods award for estimators that are now routine.
Competition from other methods candidates with broader conceptual impact.
Limitations of the estimators are well documented, such as weak instruments in persistent series and many-instruments bias.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Introduced firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, explaining exporter premia, within-industry reallocation and a new channel for gains from trade. It transformed the field and is the basis for a large body of micro-data evidence. A strong successor to the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) and Helpman's wider body of work reinforce his credit. Redding is credited but his work is mostly more recent and quantitative.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of testing and extension. The framework is the workhorse of modern trade.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views a pair award as sufficient or wants a third name (such as Redding or a co-author outside the list).
Helpman also appears in the trade-politics candidate, so credit overlap is possible.
Quantitative-trade implications for welfare gains are debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Credit Cycles (1997) formalised how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. The model underlies a large part of macro-finance and policy analysis of financial crises and balance-sheet recessions. The importance of the idea was reinforced by the 2008 crisis.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist are credited for the financial accelerator and for empirical work, but that line has already been partly recognised through the 2022 prize.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years of influence, with extensions to liquidity and monetary economics.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether the committee prefers a macro-finance award that also includes Gertler and Gilchrist.
Limited direct empirical testing of the original model, with much of the evidence indirect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with staggered pricing, the Taylor rule and the microfounded monetary policy analysis, is the dominant paradigm for central-bank thinking. Its influence on policy practice is exceptional.
assessment.attribution: Credit is diffuse and contestable. Calvo and Taylor developed pricing and contract models and the policy rule, Woodford provided the integrated theory, and Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets built the empirical and estimated versions. A three-person cap leaves out central contributors.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of development, with extensive policy use. Mature and tested, though the 2008 crisis and the post-pandemic inflation exposed limits.
uncertainties: Very hard attribution problem across a large group of contributors.
Recent inflation episodes and debates over the empirical Phillips curve.
Prior macroeconomics prizes (Lucas, Sargent/Sims, Kydland/Prescott) may reduce appetite for another monetary macro award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cities, agglomeration and housing are central to productivity, inequality and policy. This work provides microfoundations for agglomeration economies and a large body of evidence on cities, housing supply and local growth. Krugman's 2008 prize covered related theory, leaving room for empirical and microfoundations work.
assessment.attribution: Duranton and Puga are credited for the microfoundations of urban agglomeration, and Glaeser for the empirical and policy work on cities and growth. Moretti and Gyourko are strong contributors in local labour markets and housing, so a three-person selection is somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Core work spans 1990s to 2010s and the field is well established, with ongoing refinement of causal identification.
uncertainties: Credit division across five strong candidates.
Identification of agglomeration elasticities remains debated.
Uncertain whether the committee sees urban economics as a priority after the 2008 prize.
